title: STEC D+ Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome: Shiga Toxin, Microangiopathy and Supportive Care
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology

steps.say: The classic hemolytic uremic syndrome triad comprises microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.
steps.tx: Recognize the diagnostic presentation of the **STEC D+ HUS classic triad** in children following bloody diarrhea. Hemolytic uremic syndrome is formally defined by the clinical triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (Coombs-negative, characterized by fragmented red blood cells or schistocytes on peripheral blood smear), thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 150,000/mm³), and acute kidney injury manifesting with oliguria, hematuria, and azotemia.

vis.title: Classic HUS Diagnostic Triad
rows: Hb drop, schistocytes, Coombs negative, high LDH
Platelet consumption within glomerular capillary clots

steps.say: Shiga toxins bind endothelial globotriaosylceramide receptors, halting protein synthesis and triggering microvascular thrombosis.
steps.tx: Understand molecular pathogenesis involving **Shiga toxin pathogenesis and Gb3 receptors** in target tissues. Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (such as O157:H7, O26, and O104) produce Shiga toxins (Stx1 and Stx2). These toxins enter the bloodstream and bind globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) receptors abundantly expressed on glomerular endothelial cells. Receptor-mediated endocytosis delivers toxin subunits that cleave ribosomal RNA, halting protein synthesis and inciting endothelial apoptosis and microvascular thrombosis.

steps.say: Antibiotics and antimotility agents during prodromal colitis increase toxin release and elevate HUS risk up to seventeen fold.
steps.tx: Enforce strict medication avoidance to prevent the **Antibiotic hazard in STEC colitis** in children with enteritis. Antibiotics (including fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin and co-trimoxazole) and antimotility agents (such as loperamide) administered during the prodromal diarrheal phase induce bacterial SOS stress responses, increasing Shiga toxin expression and release. This dramatically elevates the risk of developing systemic HUS by up to seventeen-fold.

left.title: Strictly Prohibited Therapies
points: Up to 17-fold elevated risk of systemic HUS

right.title: Mandated Clinical Approach
points: Meticulous fluid balance and electrolyte monitoring

steps.say: Vigorous early volume expansion preserves renal microvascular perfusion and halves the need for emergency dialysis.
steps.tx: Administer aggressive fluid protocols for **Early volume expansion renal protection** during the acute diarrheal phase. Early intravenous volume expansion with isotonic saline (administered at 10-15 mL/kg/hr initially during the diarrheal prodrome) preserves renal capillary perfusion, counteracts microvascular hypoperfusion, and halves the requirement for acute renal replacement therapy in pediatric patients.

nodes.label: Halves Need for Acute Dialysis & Renal Failure

steps.say: Platelet transfusions are contraindicated because infusing platelets fuels active microvascular thrombosis in glomerular capillaries.
steps.tx: Adhere strictly to the established **Platelet transfusion restriction rule** during supportive care. Platelet transfusions are strictly contraindicated in hemolytic uremic syndrome because transfused platelets become incorporated into active glomerular microthrombi, worsening microvascular occlusion and renal ischemia. Transfusions are reserved exclusively for patients with life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage or active invasive surgical bleeding.

vis.title: Transfusion Thresholds in Pediatric HUS
rows: Transfuse slowly to maintain tissue oxygen delivery
Strictly avoid routinely; fuels microvascular thrombosis

steps.say: Diagnosis is confirmed by isolating non-sorbitol fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar or detecting toxin genes by PCR.
steps.tx: Order appropriate microbiological diagnostics through **Stx stool PCR and sorbitol-MacConkey agar** stool testing. Diagnosis is confirmed by stool culture on Sorbitol-MacConkey (SMAC) agar, where classic E. coli O157:H7 strains appear colorless due to failure to ferment sorbitol, or by stool enzyme immunoassay (EIA) and multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting Stx1 and Stx2 genes.

vis.title: Microbiological Identification of STEC
rows: Rapid screen for classic O157:H7 strains
Detection of stx1 and stx2 genes
High sensitivity, detects non-O157 STEC strains
Rapid confirmation in diarrheal stool samples

steps.say: Over fifty percent of children require acute peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis to manage anuria and fluid overload.
steps.tx: Evaluate acute indications to determine the **Indications for acute dialysis in D+ HUS** during the oliguric phase. Acute peritoneal dialysis or continuous hemodialysis is required in over fifty percent of children with D+ HUS due to refractory anuria, severe fluid overload with pulmonary edema, symptomatic uremic encephalopathy, or intractable hyperkalemia unresponsive to medical therapy.

steps.say: Up to thirty percent of survivors develop late-onset hypertension or chronic kidney disease from hyperfiltration injury.
steps.tx: Establish structured long-term outpatient follow-up for **Long-term renal sequelae surveillance** following acute recovery. Up to thirty percent of children surviving acute STEC HUS develop hypertension, proteinuria, or progressive chronic kidney disease years later due to hyperfiltration and secondary glomerulosclerosis in surviving nephrons. Long-term management requires annual blood pressure checks and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio surveillance.

vis.title: Long-Term Surveillance Protocol Post-HUS
rows: Blood pressure, urinalysis, creatinine every 3 months
Annual blood pressure, UPCR, serum creatinine
